sections.title: Jews and Violence in Antiquity
sections.description: The Passover Haggadah encodes a prominent narrative in Jewish memory, that "in each generation, they stand against us to destroy us, but the Holy One, blessed be He, rescues us from their hand." This narrative, influential in shaping international policies toward Jews and other minority groups, and in informing modern Jewish identities, consolidates all episodes of violence against Jews into a singular, enduring pattern, irrespective of period, place, cause, or those responsible. Yet in so doing, the various complex contexts and scenarios of violence against Jews are sidelined, failing to capture the different stories and experiences of particular Jews with violence. What's more, framing Jews as perennially persecuted, such narratives often neglect fascinating accounts of violence by and among Jews in antiquity. This course explores the complex relationship between ancient Jewish communities and the phenomenon of violence in the context of their historical, cultural, and religious milieux. Students will delve into key aspects of ancient Jewish history, examining narratives, responses, and interpretations of violence from various perspectives. The course asks: What conditions generated violence against Jews? When and why were Jews violent? What role did different factors – politics, religion, economy, ideology, social fissures, literature and more – play in provoking moments of violence? To what degree was violence top down versus bottom up, official versus unauthorized, widespread versus local? How did Jews respond to moments of violence?
